primary.thesis: The top score on the Arena Coding leaderboard (style control off) rises through a small number of big jumps, each one a new frontier release from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic or xAI. Each new flagship tends to debut 20 to 40 points above the previous leader, and the top of the board has drifted up roughly 80 to 100 points a year. The ladder is centred on 1580, which suggests the leader at end of September sits somewhere in the 1540s to 1560s. Q4 is usually busy for releases (holiday-season launches and year-end pushes), so at least one new flagship should land and nudge the top score past 1560. Reaching 1600 would take an unusually large jump, possibly two in a row, within about 13 weeks, with no rebasing or score compression in between. As the pool of strong models grows, Bradley-Terry scores near the top also tend to compress, which makes a 40+ point leap less likely. So the lower rung should hit and the top rung should not.

basket.reason: 1560 is the lowest rung. It is probably close to the current leader, so one routine Q4 flagship release (for example a Gemini, GPT or Claude point release) is enough to touch it. The market also resolves YES if the score is reached at any point before the deadline, which favours YES.

1600 needs a jump of roughly 40+ points over the current frontier within one quarter. Rating compression at the top and the risk that Arena changes its methodology both work against a new all-time high that large.

failure_narrative: The basket loses in one of two opposite ways. (a) Stagnation. No major lab ships a new flagship onto Arena before Dec 31, because of delayed training runs, compute or power limits, safety holds, or labs choosing to launch outside Arena. Or Arena renormalises or rebases its scores (a new anchor model, a changed methodology, a merged style-control default), which pushes the top Coding score down so it stays below 1560. C1 then loses. (b) Breakout. A step-change model, such as a next-generation Gemini or GPT trained on much larger clusters, debuts 50+ points clear of the field. Alternatively, anonymous pre-release variants posted under codenames push the top score above 1600, and C3 loses. A third route to a loss is the leaderboard going offline, or its URL or tab structure changing, which creates resolution ambiguity.
hedge_thesis: The main way the basket fails is the stagnation case: no new frontier model ships in Q4. That same world would show up in AI infrastructure and capital markets. Frontier releases are gated by getting large training clusters online, which depends on GPU deliveries, advanced-packaging (CoWoS) capacity, grid power and hyperscaler capex. If flagship launches slip past December, the likely underlying causes are datacenter or power delays, chip supply bottlenecks, or a pullback in AI capex. Those same causes would show up as weaker-than-expected data-center revenue guidance, capex cuts or deferrals at hyperscalers, and falling AI-infrastructure equities. So the hedge is that AI-infrastructure spending and sentiment disappoint in Q4 2026. It is linked through the physical compute supply chain, not through leaderboard mechanics, and it would tend to be true in exactly the worlds where the Arena top score fails to move past 1560.
